notes:
I ran out of research tools before I could cover the whole chapter. I read David Guzik's Enduring Word page only up to v. 14; for vv. 19–35 I have only search excerpts from it. I couldn't open Matthew Henry's full page (it loaded menus only), any NET Bible notes on Exodus 32, any Orthodox source (oca.org), or any material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out. Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary appear only where they turned up in excerpts.

## Notes by verse

**v. 1**
- Moses was gone 40 days (Ex 24:18). Guzik says how we handle God's delays shows our spiritual maturity. He also notes the idea started with the people, not Aaron. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Guzik quotes Cole: as Israel later wanted a human king, here they want a god "with a face." He also quotes Kaiser that "this Moses" is deliberately coarse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Barnes: the people had largely lost the faith of the patriarchs. They seem to have thought Moses had fooled them or died in the thunder on the mountain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-4.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik sets this against the offering God commanded for the tabernacle (Ex 25:1–7). Aaron collected gold for an idol before Moses could collect it for God's dwelling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: people are naturally generous toward their idols, and Christians should give even more freely to the living God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Precept Austin quotes Trapp: we often take God's gifts and make a golden calf of them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary

**v. 4**
- **Who brought you out of Egypt:** Guzik points out the absurdity. The calf did not exist the day before, yet it was praised as the god of the Exodus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- **How it was made:** commentators disagree.
  - Precept Austin and Constable think it was probably a wooden frame covered in gold (compare Isa 30:22). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/exodus-32.html
  - Coffman thinks the wording points to solid gold. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-4.html
- **Who it was meant to be:**
  - Constable, quoting others, calls the sin idolatry rather than polytheism: an attempt to picture the covenant God in a physical image. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-4.html
  - Precept Austin cites J. I. Packer: the people meant to worship the LORD and used a bull to recall His might, but the image showed nothing of His holiness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary
  - Coffman disagrees. Because the verb and noun are plural ("gods"), he says neither Aaron nor Jeroboam could have meant Jehovah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/12-28.html
- **Catholic reading:** the old Catholic Encyclopedia notes the long debate over whether this was outright idolatry or a visible image of Yahweh, and says the text seems to favour the second view. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tce/a/aaron.html
  - Its "Golden Calf" article says most writers follow Philo and the early Fathers in seeing an Egyptian origin. It notes a difficulty: an Egyptian god is an unlikely candidate for the god who brought Israel out of Egypt. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/golden-calf
- **Modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says the account of Jeroboam's two calves in Kings closely resembles Exodus 32. Many scholars think those calves were familiar stands for the invisible Yahweh enthroned above them, like the cherubim in Judah. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-sanctuaries-at-dan-and-bethel/
- Easton's dictionary (on the NET Bible site) suggests the calf copied Moloch rather than the Egyptian Apis. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=CALF

**v. 5**
- Guzik: building an altar made things worse, because it honoured the idol with sacrifice. "A feast to the LORD" shows the people were not consciously rejecting the LORD. They thought they could honour Him *through* the calf. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary is kinder to Aaron. It suggests he may have used the LORD's name and a one-day delay to stall, hoping the people would remember the ban on images or that Moses would return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/exodus-32.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik, citing Cole and Kaiser: the Hebrew word for "play" (here "revelry") implies drunken sexual immorality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Paul quotes this verse in 1 Cor 10:7 as a warning against idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/exodus-32.html
- Kingcomments applies it to worship planned to please the worshippers, where the Lord's name is used but His Word is not consulted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/exodus-32.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik: by calling Israel "*your* people," God hints that He is disowning them. He knows exactly what happened, even quoting their words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Precept Austin: the word for "corrupted" is used elsewhere of Israel's decline after a judge died (Judg 2:19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: "stiff-necked" is Cole's farmer's picture of an animal that won't answer the rope. God's offer would have made Moses a new Abraham. "Leave Me alone" implied that if Moses did nothing, judgment would follow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/

**vv. 11–13**
- Guzik sees four appeals in Moses' prayer:
  - he gives the people back to God;
  - he appeals to grace (God freed them without their deserving it);
  - he appeals to God's glory (what will the Egyptians say?);
  - he appeals to God's faithfulness to His promises to the patriarchs.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Barnes: this was a test of whether Moses loved his own glory, as founder of a great nation, more than his people. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/exodus/32-32.html

**v. 14 — God "relented" (a point where teachers really differ)**
- Guzik says the language describes God's actions as they appeared to Moses. Moses' prayer did not change God; it moved the people from a place of judgment to a place of mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Bible.org: God's "repenting" involves no sin and no wavering. It only *seems* to change from our point of view, the way we say the sun "sets." https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-3-man-who-caused-god-repent-exodus-327-14-30-35-331-6-12-17
- Constable: God's character does not change, but His plan allows several acceptable courses, and He took a different one because Moses prayed. He criticises "openness of God" teachers. In his view they treat this as a deeper change in God that He had not foreseen, stressing human free will at the expense of God's sovereignty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-14.html
- GotQuestions says open theism uses this verse, but answers that it is God describing Himself in terms we can understand. https://www.gotquestions.org/open-theism.html
- Precept Austin quotes a writer (Chisholm, apparently) who goes further: Moses really did weaken God's resolve, showing that God responds to human pleading. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary
- A Monergism article (Reformed) poses the problem sharply: taken at face value, it would mean Moses showed God a better way. I only saw the opening, not its conclusion. https://www.monergism.com/does-god-change-his-mind

**vv. 15–16**
- Hamilton, quoted by Precept Austin: the stress on God making the tablets contrasts what God makes with what Aaron makes. Both are destroyed, one by smashing, the other by burning and grinding. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary

**vv. 17–19**
- Precept Austin: the last time Israel sang and danced was after the Red Sea (Ex 15:20–21). Now they do the same for an idol. Dancing itself is not condemned, only dancing to an idol. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary
- Constable: breaking the tablets symbolised that Israel had broken the covenant. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/exodus-32.html

**v. 20**
- Guzik gives four reasons for making them drink it:
  - to show the "god" was nothing;
  - to destroy it completely;
  - to make the people bear an immediate consequence;
  - to make the gold unusable.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Constable: Moses dishonoured the calf as well as destroying it. Some see an old Canaanite pattern for describing the total destruction of an enemy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/exodus-32.html
- Kingcomments: it was meant to bring home to the people, deep inside, how foolish they had been. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/exodus-32.html

**vv. 21–24**
- Clarke calls Aaron's excuse a "silly and ridiculous subterfuge." Gill notes he talks as if the calf made itself, and that Jewish tradition blamed magic or Satan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-24.html
- The detail in v. 4 about the engraving tool exposes the lie. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-24.html
- Precept Austin: Aaron broke the first, second and ninth commandments, and probably the third. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary
- Constable quotes a sermon application: people still blame "the furnace" (the trend of the times) for their own choices. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/exodus-32.html

**v. 25**
- Precept Austin: the details aren't given, but the behaviour was unruly and ungodly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary

**vv. 26–29 — the Levites**
- Matthew Henry: Moses raised his "banner" against the idolaters' standard, the calf. "Slay his brother" meant those the Levites knew had taken an active part, even close relatives. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_032.cfm
- Barnes: their zeal anticipated their formal consecration as ministers of the sanctuary. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/exodus/32-32.html
- **Do the Levites earn their role here?** Teachers differ.
  - Easton's dictionary: the tribe first became distinct here, receiving the religious role of the firstborn because of its zeal. https://ccel.org/e/easton/ebd2/cache/ebd2.html3
  - GotQuestions disagrees: God had already made Levi priestly *before* this (Ex 28:1–4). https://www.gotquestions.org/Levitical-priesthood.html
- **Catholic reading:** Catholic Answers says the earlier priesthood of the firstborn passed to the Levites after the golden calf. It uses this in arguing for a ministerial priesthood. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-biblical-blueprint-for-the-priesthood
- **Why wasn't Aaron punished?** GotQuestions suggests:
  - he was punished later, dying outside the land and losing two sons;
  - he had already been chosen as high priest;
  - as a son of Levi he was among those who repented.
  https://www.gotquestions.org/Aaron-golden-calf.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes God kept His choice of Aaron despite the sin. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/aaron

**vv. 30–32 — "Blot me out of Your book" (a point where teachers really differ)**
- Guzik: Moses offered to be *damned* in place of the people, feeling no animal sacrifice could cover such sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- Pulpit, citing Keil: the book lists the righteous and secures life before God, including eternal life. Moses was willing to bear their guilt in this world and the next, like Paul in Rom 9:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-32.htm
- The Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): Moses valued God's glory above his own salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-32.htm
- Others (Benson, the Cambridge Bible) read it as "let me die" (compare Num 11:15), the book being the register of the living. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-32.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): it was God's list of those who would enter Canaan. Moses did not want to enter without his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-32.html
- John Piper (Baptist, Reformed): v. 33 seems to make the book insecure. He concludes that in Exodus the book is probably the list of Israel's living, and being blotted out means dying. The meaning develops later in Scripture into the book of eternal life. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/late-night-meditations-on-the-book-of-life
- A Bible Hub study note keeps both truths: believers are secure, yet the warnings are real. True believers persevere, while false members may be erased. It sees Moses pointing to Christ, the only substitute God accepts. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_blot_me_out_in_Exodus_32_32.htm
- The Bible Says (on Blue Letter Bible) offers another option: Moses may have been offering to lose the *rewards* due for his faithfulness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-32-v30-35.cfm

**v. 33**
- Henry: God would not take Moses at his word. Only those who sin wilfully are blotted out, not the innocent in place of the guilty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-32.html
- Guzik: God spared the nation but kept the right to judge individuals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/

**v. 34**
- Keil (via Bible Hub): God turns down Moses' offer but promises the nation will continue under His angel, with punishment put off until the day He settles accounts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/32-32.htm
- Benson: when God later punishes other sins, He will count this one too. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-35.html

**v. 35**
- Ellicott: probably not a single epidemic but various sufferings inflicted as punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-35.html
- Clarke and Henry both cite the Jewish saying that every later affliction contained a particle of the golden calf's dust. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-35.html
- Calvin: the calf is called Aaron's work and the people's, so the guilt was shared. Currid notes "they did" and "had made" use the same verb, making them co-conspirators. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/32-35.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-32-commentary
